_comment: Every expectation the bench tools check - which microphone leads which
for a clap from a named direction, and by how many samples - is derived
from the positions below, not written out by hand somewhere in a script.
A new board is then a --geometry flag, not a code change, and there is one
place where a mismeasured baseline can be wrong.
Channel order everywhere in this project is [M1 M2 M3 M4].
Axes: +x = east, +y = north. North is the forward / USB-cable edge.
Positions are millimetres from the array centre, in the array plane.
Detection is geometry-free. Nothing in this file feeds the detector.
It is read by the bench tools (quad_tap, quad_analysis, field_day,
field_test) and by the offline spatial mini-synth, all of which are
instruments, not the instrument under test.

breadboard_plus_v1.name: breadboard_plus_v1
notes: Hand-built on breadboard, so the tolerance is a hand tolerance.
M1/M2 share I2S bus A and M3/M4 share bus B, which is why the N-S
axis and the inter-bus start offset are confounded on this build and
the E-W axis is not. That is a property of the wiring, not the
geometry, and it is the reason S4 (overhead clap) exists: an overhead
source has zero acoustic delay on every baseline, so anything left is

pcb_rev_a2.name: pcb_rev_a2
pcb_rev_a2.status: PCB rev A2, positions from the board design, not measured
notes: A photo-plotted board, so 0.1 mm rather than 0.5 mm.
The longest baseline becomes the 79.20 mm diagonal, which moves the
half-wavelength crossover down from ~2813 Hz to ~2165 Hz. The comb
score reaches to 7800 Hz, so more of the scored teeth sit above the
crossover on this board than on the breadboard, which makes the CX-B
/ CX-C combiner question more relevant on the PCB, not less.
